a: Basketry is the ancient craft of weaving flexible plant materials into containers, mats, furniture, and sculptural objects, dating back over 10,000 years and found in virtually every culture worldwide as one of humanity's earliest crafts. Materials are broadly classified as natural fibers harvested and prepared specifically for weaving: reed (also called rattan core, the inner pith of the rattan vine) is the most common commercial basket weaving material, available in round and flat widths, easy to work with, and takes dye well; willow (osier) is harvested from coppiced willow trees, soaked to become flexible, and used in traditional European basketry for strong, durable baskets; rattan (the outer skin of the rattan vine) is strong and flexible, used for furniture and structural basket elements; bamboo is split into thin strips for weaving in Asian basketry traditions; seagrass and sisal are coarse natural fibers used for rustic baskets and mats; and raffia (palm leaf fibers) is soft and pliable for coiled basketry and decorative accents. In coiled basketry, the foundation is typically a core of bundled grass, pine needles, or fabric strips, wrapped and stitched with a stronger fiber. Basketry was historically essential for storage, transport, fishing (traps and creels), agriculture (harvest baskets), and trade, with distinct regional styles—from Native American coiled and twined baskets and African coiled grass baskets to European willow wickerwork and Asian split bamboo baskets—that continue to influence contemporary basket makers.

a: Basket weaving techniques are categorized by the structural method of interlacing fibers. Coiling is one of the oldest techniques, where a foundation core (bunched grass, pine needles, or fabric cord) is spiraled and stitched together with a threaded needle and wrapping fiber—each stitch passing through the previous coil to lock it in place, creating sturdy, sculptural forms with patterns formed by colored wrapping threads. Twining uses paired flexible weavers twisted around rigid warp stakes in a figure-eight motion, with each row of twining pressed tightly against the previous one, allowing patterns through colored weavers and variations like plain twining, wrapped twining, and braided twining. Plaiting (also called braiding or checker weave) interlaces flat or round strands at right angles in an over-one, under-one pattern, similar to textile weaving, producing flat or gently curved mats and baskets with checkered patterns. Wicker or stake-and-strand weaving is the most common basket technique: rigid upright stakes (the warp) are inserted into a base, soaked soft weavers (the weft) are woven alternately over and under the stakes in a continuous spiral, with the rows packed tight using a weaving gauge or bodkin to maintain consistent spacing. Essential basketry tools are relatively simple: a sharp knife or pruners for cutting materials, a bodkin or awl for opening gaps between weaves, a weaving gauge (a flat stick the width of the desired gap) for maintaining even spacing, a lapboard or work surface with clips to hold stakes in place while weaving, soaking tubs or spray bottles to keep fibers flexible during work, and wooden base molds or forms for shaping specific basket styles. Techniques for finishing include tucking and trimming ends, adding a rim (a bundle of reed or willow lashed around the top edge with a separate binding element), and adding handles by inserting thicker rods into the weave and wrapping them with flexible weavers.

a: Baskets are categorized by their construction method and regional tradition. Rib baskets (also called hooped baskets) use a single curved rib as the warp, with weavers woven across it, producing oval or D-shaped forms traditionally used for gathering eggs, fruit, or sewing supplies. Melon baskets (also called ribbed baskets or staved baskets) have multiple curved ribs radiating from a central base block, creating a round, melon-like shape with a handle arching over the top—a classic Appalachian and Shaker form. Nantucket baskets are finely woven, tightly packed rattan baskets with a wooden bottom and mold-made shape, traditionally made by sailors on Nantucket Island with ivory fittings and tight-fitting lids, now highly collectible as handbags and decorative pieces. Shaker baskets are characterized by clean, functional lines, fine weaving with narrow reed or tape, and careful wood bottom construction—designed for utility in Shaker communities with simple, elegant proportions. Market baskets (also called picnic or shopping baskets) are large, open rectangular or oval baskets with a broad central handle, woven in a sturdy wicker or stake-and-strand pattern for carrying goods. Common weaving patterns include the basic over-one under-one checker pattern, over-two under-two patterns for speed and texture, herringbone (diagonal woven pattern), triple-twist (three weavers twined for decorative banding), and various arrow and diamond patterns created by varying which warp stakes are picked up by the weaver. Decorative weaves include the star weave on basket bottoms, the honeycomb weave (alternating high and low stakes for a hexagonal pattern), and lattice weave (diagonal strips interwoven over a base layer for decorative walls and lids).

a: Beginners should start with a simple round-bottom market basket or a small coil basket using pre-dyed commercial reed, which requires no harvesting or preparation and is available in consistent widths from craft suppliers. The basic process begins with cutting bottom stakes to length, soaking them for 10-15 minutes until pliable, inserting them into a pre-made wooden or reed base (or weaving a base from crossed stakes in a star pattern), bending the stakes upward to create the sides, then weaving round reed weavers alternately over and under the upright stakes, packing each row down with a weaving gauge. The rim is formed by adding a thick bundle of two to four round reeds around the top edge, clipping the ends of the stakes over the rim bundle, and lashing them in place with a separate binding weaver (a French randing, or a simple over-and-over wrap). Handles are added by inserting two or three thick reeds into the weave on opposite sides, bending them to shape, and wrapping them tightly with a soaked flat or round reed weaver. Caring for baskets involves keeping them away from direct heat and sunlight (which causes drying and brittleness), cleaning with a soft brush or lightly damp cloth (never soaking), and conditioning natural reed with a light mist of water if fibers become dry. Repairs involve replacing broken stakes by cutting them off at the base and weaving in new ones of matching size, or splicing broken weavers by tapering the ends and tucking them into adjacent weave with glue. Dyeing is done with commercial reed dye or fabric dye dissolved in hot water—submerge the reed for 10-30 minutes for desired color intensity, rinse, and dry before weaving, or apply dye after weaving with a brush for selective coloring.
